newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's vote continues normally, few incidents.
newsitem.headline: Albania's vote continues normally, few incidents.

text.p: Voting proceeded briskly on Sunday in Albania's make-or-break general election, with only sporadic incidents disrupting what many view as the only way to halt the violence which pitched the country into near-anarchy.

Both president Sali Berisha, trying to retain his Democratic Party's stranglehold on parliament, and his main rival, Socialist leader Fatos Nano, said after casting their votes that they would respect the outcome.
Both men forecast victory for their parties in a tough campaign, Albania's fourth since the 1990 fall of communism.

The official ATA news agency reported turnout of 55 percent by early afternoon in many districts, about the same as last year's general election won by Berisha's Democrats but denounced as unfair by international observers.
By lunch time, in scorching heat, queues had formed at most polling stations in the capital.
In the south, focal point of unrest which has killed 1,500 people, no major incidents were reported. One gang leader in the port of Vlore turned up to vote in tails and bow tie.
"I will fully recognise the elections," Berisha said in English after voting in a Tirana classroom full of reporters.
Berisha, president since 1992, was coy about whether he would stay in office if the Socialists scored a big victory. It was too early, he said, to consider "cohabitation" in Albania.
Nano said the election was the first step of Albania's integration into Europe, seven years after the collapse of one of eastern Europe's most repressive communist regimes.
"These elections are of extraordinary importance," he said. "This will be a society of free citizens no different from other European nations. Tomorrow will be a new day."
Catherine Lalumiere, official of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe helping oversee the vote, said she was pleased with what she saw at polling stations.
She told voters that any repeat of last year's irregularities would result in foreign aid remaining frozen.
The OSCE has said it is unrealistic for normal Western standards to be attained in Albania's election.
Both Berisha's Democrat and the Socialists complained of irregularities, mostly voters left off registration lists.
Some incidents were more serious.
The spokesman for the 7,000-strong Multinational Protection Force sent to restore a measure of order in April said armed men had stolen ballots from a village near the port of Durres.
ATA said voting was suspended in parts of Lezhe, north of Tirana, after a similar incident. It said police had thwarted at least four other attacks.

In Mat district, central Albania, no voting was taking place as ballot papers had not been delivered. The OSCE had to reprint papers for 10 districts 48 hours before the vote after election officials complained of errors.
Predicting the outcome is virtually impossible.
Berisha was initially lionised by the West for promoting free market policies in the aftermath of communist rule but has been criticised for increasingly authoritarian rule.
Many Albanians blame him for the collapse of five fraudulent investment schemes earlier this year which sparked the uprising, initially by furious savers.
"Anyone who wins should throw out 80-90 percent of the system to get rid of this intolerable regime," said Ramazan in his 50s. "We cannot survive with Berisha's regime any more."
Berisha's Democrats portray themselves as guarantors of stability and say the Socialists were behind the violence.
The election campaign was conducted under a state of emergency imposed on March 2 to try to quell the unrest. A 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew has been lifted just for election day.

More than 1,000 candidates from 27 parties are vying for 155 seats -- 115 to be decided in two-round majority races and the rest by a proportional system. The Democrats hold 122 of 140 seats in the outgoing parliament.
Voters were also asked in a referendum whether they favoured restoring the monarchy. But few believe King Leka I, back from exile, has much chance of returning to the throne.
